title: Power Sharing
short: Belgium and Sri Lanka, and the four forms of power sharing.
lede: Two case studies and one list of four forms. The shortest route to 20 marks in Social Science starts here.
lens: **3–5 marks.** The Belgium and Sri Lanka comparison and the forms of power sharing are the set questions.
Answers are **point-based**: five distinct points for a 5-mark answer, each with a heading. Long paragraphs score less.
concepts: **1. The case of Belgium.** Belgium is a small country in Europe, smaller in area than Haryana, with a population just over one crore. It has a **complex ethnic composition**: 59% live in the **Flemish** region and speak **Dutch**, 40% in the **Wallonia** region and speak **French**, and 1% speak German. In the capital **Brussels**, 80% speak French and 20% Dutch — the French-speaking minority there was relatively rich and powerful. Between **1932 and 1968** the constitution was amended **four times** to work out an arrangement that would enable everyone to live together: an equal number of Dutch- and French-speaking ministers in the central government; many powers given to **state governments** of the two regions, which are not subordinate to the central government; **Brussels** given a separate government with equal representation for both groups; and a third kind of government — the **community government** — elected by people belonging to one language group (Dutch, French or German-speaking) regardless of where they live, with power over culture, education and language.

**2. The case of Sri Lanka.** An island nation with about 74% **Sinhala** speakers and 18% **Tamils**, most of them concentrated in the north and east. In **1956** an act was passed to recognise **Sinhala as the only official language**, disregarding Tamil. The governments followed preferential policies that favoured Sinhala applicants for university positions and government employment, and the new constitution stipulated that the state shall **protect and foster Buddhism**. Sri Lankan Tamils demanded recognition of Tamil as an official language, regional autonomy and equal opportunity. Their demand for a separate Tamil state, **Tamil Eelam**, led to a civil war that began in the 1980s and continued until **2009**, leaving thousands dead and damaging the social, cultural and economic life of the country.

**3. Why power sharing is desirable.** **Prudential reasons:** power sharing reduces the possibility of conflict between social groups; since social conflict often leads to violence and political instability, sharing power is a good way to ensure the stability of the political order. Imposing the will of the majority community over others may seem attractive in the short run but undermines national unity in the long run. **Moral reasons:** power sharing is the very spirit of democracy. A democratic government must share power with those affected by its exercise and who have to live with its effects; people have a right to be consulted on how they are to be governed. Legitimate government is one in which citizens, through participation, acquire a stake in the system.

**4. Forms of power sharing.** (a) **Horizontal distribution** — among organs of government such as the legislature, executive and judiciary, which allows one organ to check the others; this is the **system of checks and balances**. (b) **Vertical distribution** — among governments at different levels: the Union or central government, the state governments and local bodies such as municipalities and panchayats. The constitution specifies how the powers of each are to be exercised. (c) **Among social groups** — **community government** in Belgium, and **reserved constituencies** in assemblies and parliaments in India for weaker sections and women. (d) **Among political parties, pressure groups and movements** — **coalition governments** when no single party gets a clear majority, so two or more parties share power.

**5. India's arrangements.** Power sharing is built into the constitution: between the Union and the states through the **Union List, State List and Concurrent List**; between organs through an independent judiciary that can strike down laws that violate the constitution; through **reserved seats** for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and, in local bodies, one-third of seats for women; and through coalition governments at the centre and in the states.
tricks: - **Belgium accommodated, Sri Lanka imposed.** Those two words are the entire comparison — then add three details for each.
- **Four forms: horizontal, vertical, social groups, political parties.** *'H-V-S-P'.*
- **Prudential = practical benefit; Moral = it is right in itself.** Always label which is which.
mistakes: - Giving Belgium's language shares the wrong way round. **59% Flemish (Dutch)**, 40% Walloon (French), 1% German.
- Saying the Sri Lankan civil war ended in 2005. It ended in **2009**.
- Confusing **horizontal** (organs at the same level) with **vertical** (levels of government).

qa.q: What is the difference between prudential and moral reasons for power sharing?
qa.a: Prudential reasons stress the good consequences of power sharing — it reduces conflict between social groups, ensures the stability of political order and prevents violence and political instability. Moral reasons stress the intrinsic worth of power sharing — that people have a right to be consulted on how they are to be governed, and that a legitimate government is one in which citizens acquire a stake in the system through participation. Prudential reasons are about outcomes; moral reasons are about principles.

qa.q: Describe the major steps taken towards power sharing in Belgium.
a: **Equal representation in the central government:** the constitution prescribes an equal number of Dutch-speaking and French-speaking ministers, so no single community can take decisions unilaterally.

**Devolution to the regions:** many powers of the central government were given to the state governments of the Flemish and Walloon regions, and these regional governments are not subordinate to the central government.
**Brussels:** the capital was given a separate government with equal representation for both the French- and Dutch-speaking groups.

**Community government:** a third kind of government was set up, elected by people belonging to one language group — Dutch, French or German-speaking — irrespective of where they live, with power over cultural, educational and language-related issues.
This arrangement, worked out between 1932 and 1968 through four constitutional amendments, prevented civic strife and the division of the country on linguistic lines.

qa.q: What were the majoritarian measures adopted by the Sri Lankan government? What were their consequences?
a: In **1956** an act was passed to recognise **Sinhala as the only official language**, disregarding Tamil.
Successive governments followed **preferential policies** that favoured Sinhala applicants for university positions and government employment.
The new constitution stipulated that the state shall **protect and foster Buddhism**.

**Consequences:** the Sri Lankan Tamils felt that none of the major political parties, led by the Buddhist Sinhala leaders, was sensitive to their language and culture. Their demand for recognition of Tamil as an official language, regional autonomy and equal opportunity was repeatedly denied, and the demand for a separate Tamil Eelam grew. This led to a **civil war** that lasted until 2009, in which thousands of people were killed and the social, cultural and economic life of the country was badly affected.

qa.q: What are the different forms of power sharing in modern democracies? Give one example of each.
qa.a: **Horizontal distribution** among organs of government — legislature, executive and judiciary, as in India, where the judiciary can review the acts of the legislature. **Vertical distribution** among governments at different levels — Union, state and local governments in India. **Distribution among social groups** — the community government in Belgium and reserved constituencies for weaker sections and women in India. **Distribution among political parties** — coalition governments formed by two or more parties when no single party gains a clear majority.

qa.q: What is a system of checks and balances?
qa.a: It is the arrangement in which the organs of government — legislature, executive and judiciary — are placed at the same level but each exercises a check on the others. The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them and the judiciary can declare a law invalid if it violates the constitution. Because of these checks no organ can exercise unlimited power, and this horizontal distribution of power is a basic feature of democracy.

title: Federalism
short: Coming together and holding together, the three lists, and decentralisation.
lede: Learn the three lists, the two routes to federalism, and the 73rd and 74th Amendments. Those three things are the chapter.
lens: **3–5 marks.** The Union List, State List and Concurrent List with subjects is a set question; decentralisation through the 1992 amendment is the other.
Case-based questions give a dispute between the centre and a state and ask you to name the list involved and who decides.
concepts: **1. What is federalism?** A system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and various constituent units of the country. Usually a federation has **two levels of government**: one for the entire country, responsible for subjects of common interest, and governments at the level of provinces or states, looking after much of the day-to-day governing. In a **unitary** system there is only one level of government, or the sub-units are subordinate to the central government. Both levels have their own legislature, executive and judiciary, and each is separately answerable to the people.

**2. Two routes to a federation.** **Coming together** — independent states come together on their own to form a bigger unit, increasing their security while retaining some sovereignty; examples are the **USA, Switzerland and Australia**. **Holding together** — a large country decides to share its power between the constituent states and the national government, with the centre tending to be more powerful; examples are **India, Spain and Belgium**. India is a holding-together federation, but the constitution does not use the word *federation* — the Indian Union is based on the principles of federalism.

**3. The constitutional scheme.** The constitution distributes legislative powers between the Union and the states through three lists. **Union List** (about 100 subjects) — subjects of national importance such as defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications and currency; only Parliament can legislate. **State List** (about 61 subjects) — subjects of state and local importance such as police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation; only the state legislature can legislate. **Concurrent List** (about 52 subjects) — subjects of common interest such as education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession; both can legislate, but if the two laws conflict, the **central law prevails**. **Residuary subjects** — those that came up after the constitution was made, such as computer software — fall to the **Union**. **Union Territories** such as Chandigarh, Lakshadweep and Delhi do not have the powers of a state; they are run directly by the Union government.

**4. How federalism works in practice.** The constitution laid down the principle, but its success depends on the nature of politics. Three features stand out: **linguistic states** — boundaries were redrawn so that people who spoke the same language lived in the same state, which strengthened unity and made administration easier, though it also created disputes; **language policy** — Hindi was declared the official language but only about 40% of Indians speak it, and 21 other languages were recognised as **scheduled languages**, with English continuing as an additional official language; and **centre-state relations** — in the early years the same party ruled both the centre and most states, so state governments did not exercise their rights fully; since the 1990s, **coalition governments** at the centre have led to a new culture of power sharing and respect for the autonomy of state governments, and the **Supreme Court** has made it difficult for the centre to dismiss state governments on political grounds.

**5. Decentralisation in India.** Decentralisation is the transfer of power from the central and state governments to **local government**. It rests on the idea that there are a large number of problems best settled at the local level, that people have better knowledge of problems in their localities, and that direct participation in decision-making is a way to train citizens in democratic habits. **Panchayati Raj** existed in a limited way earlier, but a major step was taken in **1992** with the constitutional amendment that made the **third tier** of democracy more powerful and effective: it is now **constitutionally mandatory to hold regular elections** to local government bodies; **seats are reserved** for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes; **at least one-third of all positions are reserved for women**; an independent **State Election Commission** has been created to conduct these elections; and state governments are required to **share some powers and revenue** with local bodies.

**6. Rural and urban local bodies.** **Gram panchayat** — the decision-making body for a village, consisting of elected members and the **sarpanch** who is the president of the panchayat and the political head. **Panchayat samiti (block or mandal)** — the group of all gram panchayats in a block, headed by a president or chairperson. **Zilla parishad** — the district-level body, whose chairperson is the political head of the district. **Municipalities** govern urban areas, headed by a **municipal chairperson**; in big cities a **municipal corporation** is headed by a **mayor**.

**7. Federalism and the special case of states.** Some states enjoy special provisions. **Article 370** gave special status to Jammu and Kashmir until it was revoked in **2019**; the north-eastern states such as Nagaland, Mizoram and Manipur enjoy considerable autonomy; and **Article 371** contains special provisions for several states. India's federalism is thus flexible, and the **NITI Aayog** and the **GST Council** are examples of the centre and states working together — the GST Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and includes state finance ministers.
tricks: - **Union List = national, State List = local, Concurrent = both.** If a subject matters to the whole country (defence, currency) it is Union; if it is local (police, agriculture) it is State.
- **Conflict in the Concurrent List = the central law prevails.** Always add this line — it is a marked step.
- **1992 amendment = regular elections, reservation (SC/ST/OBC, one-third women), State Election Commission, sharing of powers and revenue.** Four points, four marks.
mistakes: - Saying the Indian constitution uses the word 'federation'. It does not; the Indian Union is based on federal principles.
- Putting education in the State List. Education was moved to the **Concurrent List** in 1976.
- Forgetting **residuary subjects** go to the Union — computer software is the standard example.

qa.q: Distinguish between 'coming together' and 'holding together' federations with two examples each.
qa.a: In a coming-together federation, independent states come together on their own to form a bigger unit, pooling sovereignty while retaining their identity — the USA, Switzerland and Australia. In a holding-together federation, a large country divides power between the constituent states and the national government, and the centre tends to be more powerful — India, Spain and Belgium.

qa.q: Describe how legislative powers are distributed between the Union and the states in India.
a: **Union List:** about 100 subjects of national importance such as defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications and currency. Only Parliament can make laws on them, because uniform policy is needed for the whole country.
**State List:** about 61 subjects of state and local importance such as police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation. Ordinarily only the state legislature can make laws on these.

**Concurrent List:** about 52 subjects of common interest to both, such as education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession. Both Parliament and the state legislatures can make laws, but if the two conflict, the central law prevails.
**Residuary subjects:** subjects that came up after the constitution was made, such as computer software, fall under the jurisdiction of the Union government.

qa.q: What major step was taken in 1992 towards decentralisation in India?
a: Before 1992, elections to local bodies were not held regularly, and local bodies did not have adequate powers or resources of their own. The constitutional amendment of 1992 made the third tier of democracy far more powerful and effective.
**Regular elections** to local government bodies are now constitutionally mandatory.
**Seats are reserved** in these bodies for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.
**At least one-third of all positions are reserved for women**.
An independent institution called the **State Election Commission** has been created in each state to conduct panchayat and municipal elections.
State governments are required to **share some powers and revenue** with local government bodies, so that local bodies have the means to function.

qa.q: Explain any three features of federalism practised in India.
qa.a: **Linguistic states** — the boundaries of old states were changed and new states created so that people who speak the same language live in the same state; this made administration easier and strengthened national unity. **Language policy** — Hindi was declared the official language, but because only about 40% of Indians speak it, the constitution recognised 21 other languages as scheduled languages and allowed English to continue as an additional official language. **Centre-state relations** — the rise of coalition governments at the centre since the 1990s has created a new culture of power sharing and respect for the autonomy of state governments, and the judiciary has made it harder to dismiss state governments for political reasons.

qa.q: Why is decentralisation considered a good idea in a democracy?
qa.a: Because there are a large number of problems and issues that are best settled at the local level, such as local planning, sanitation and water supply; people have better knowledge of the problems in their own localities and can take better decisions about how to spend money; and direct participation in local decision-making is a way to train citizens in the habits of democracy and to build a democratic culture.

title: Gender, Religion and Caste
short: Gender inequality in politics, communalism, and the caste–politics relationship.
lede: Three sections in one chapter: women in politics, religion and communalism, and caste. Each one carries a set 3- or 5-mark answer.
lens: **Among the surest marks in Political Science.** The definition of communalism and the two faces of the caste–politics relationship are asked almost every year.
Learn the **three sections as three separate answers**, each with its own list of points — the paper usually asks only one of them.
concepts: **1. Gender and the sexual division of labour.** Girls and boys are brought up differently: women do the housework and look after children, men work outside the home for wages. This division of work is based on social expectation, not on biology, and it is where **gender inequality** begins. Because work outside the home is paid and visible while work at home is unpaid and unseen, women's contribution is undervalued.

**2. The public and the private.** Politics is organised in the **public sphere** — parties, elected bodies, government, law — while the **private sphere** of home and family was thought to be outside politics altogether. Women's role was confined to the private sphere, so politics came to be seen as a man's world. The divide is **patriarchal**: a system that values men more and gives them power over women.

**3. What women face.** **Literacy:** about 65 per cent of women are literate against about 82 per cent of men (Census 2011). **Wages:** women are paid less than men for the same work, which is why the **Equal Remuneration Act, 1976** requires equal wages for equal work. **Preference for sons:** sex-selective abortion has lowered the child sex ratio in many states. **Violence and burden:** harassment, domestic violence and the unequal load of housework. In almost every field, far fewer women reach the top than their share in the population would suggest.

**4. Women in political office.** In the **Lok Sabha**, women have never been more than about **14 per cent** of the members, and state assemblies are similar — well below the world average. **Local bodies show that reservation works:** one-third of the seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women (several states have raised this to half), and today more than a million women hold elected positions in rural and urban local bodies. In **2023** Parliament passed the **106th Constitutional Amendment**, reserving one-third of the seats in the Lok Sabha and the state assemblies for women; it takes effect after the next census and delimitation. Studies of panchayats find that women raise issues of drinking water, fuel, fodder and health, and that their presence changes decisions rather than merely adding numbers.

**5. Religion, politics and communalism.** Religion enters politics when the beliefs of one religion dominate political life, when one community seeks to dominate another, and when parties are formed on religious lines. **Communalism** is the belief that people who follow the same religion have common secular interests, and that people of different religions have separate and opposed interests. It has **four faces**: everyday religious prejudice and stereotypes; the desire to dominate other religious communities; the political dominance of the majority religion; and the demand for separate political units or parties for each religion. Communal politics turns dangerous when religion is treated as the only identity, when elections are fought on religious appeals, and when it spills over into violence.

**6. India is a secular state.** The Constitution gives no special status to any religion, allows every person the freedom to profess, practise and propagate a religion of their choice, prohibits discrimination on the ground of religion, and permits the state to intervene in religious matters **to ensure equality** — abolishing untouchability, for instance, and making laws for social reform. The Indian state is therefore neither hostile to religion nor walled off from it: it keeps a **principled distance**, and that is what makes equality possible in a multi-religious society.

**7. Caste and politics.** Caste is a hereditary system of graded inequality fixed by birth, and for centuries it decided access to education, work and power. **Caste in politics:** parties choose candidates with an eye to the dominant caste of a constituency, voters' choices are shaped by caste, and governments are formed keeping caste arithmetic in mind. **Politics in caste:** politics has also sharpened caste identity — castes have organised into associations and asserted themselves to claim a share of power, which is how OBCs and Dalits entered politics in large numbers.

**8. But caste does not decide everything.** No parliamentary constituency has a majority of a single caste, so every party has to win votes across castes; no party wins the votes of every voter of a caste; no caste votes as one block; and voters weigh the performance of the government and the appeal of the leader along with caste. Caste inequality has not ended, but caste alone cannot win an election.
tricks: - **Three sections, three lists:** gender (work, wages, seats), religion (communalism and secularism), caste (caste in politics, politics in caste).
- **Communalism in one line:** the same religion means common secular interests; different religions means opposed interests.
- **Numbers to quote:** Equal Remuneration Act 1976, one-third of local body seats for women, one-third for the Lok Sabha and assemblies under the 106th Amendment (2023).
- **'Caste in politics' — caste shapes elections. 'Politics in caste' — politics sharpens caste identity.** The first word tells you what is doing the shaping.
mistakes: - Calling the Indian state **anti-religious**. Secularism here is a **principled distance**: the state can and does intervene in religion to end inequality.
- Treating **communalism** as simply being religious. Communalism begins only when religion becomes the basis of a nation and of rival political interests.
- Writing that caste is finished because caste discrimination is banned. Discrimination is banned and declining, but caste **identity** is still politically active.
- Reading the chapter as **women's issues only**. The marks are for the sexual division of labour, patriarchy and representation.

qa.q: What is the sexual division of labour and how does it lead to gender inequality?
qa.a: The sexual division of labour is the arrangement in which women do the housework, cook and look after children while men work outside the home for wages. It rests on social expectation, not on biology. Because paid work outside is treated as real work while the unpaid work at home is not counted at all, women's contribution is undervalued. That is where gender inequality begins: it keeps women out of the public sphere and out of better-paid, higher-status work.

qa.q: What is communalism? Explain any three forms in which it appears in politics.
a: **Communalism** is the belief that people who follow the same religion have common secular interests, and that people of different religions have separate and opposed interests. It is the most common form in which religion is used in politics.
**Everyday prejudice:** religious prejudices, stereotypes about other communities and the belief that one's own religion is superior.
**Domination:** the desire to establish the dominance of one's own religious community over others and to use state power for it.
**Majoritarian dominance:** the belief that the majority community should rule, which turns religion into the basis of political power.
**Separate political units or parties:** demanding a separate state, or forming parties on religious lines.
Communal politics turns violent when religion is treated as the only identity and elections are fought on religious appeals.

qa.q: What does it mean to say that India is a secular state?
a: The Constitution gives no special status to any religion — there is no official religion.
Every person has the freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion of their choice.
Discrimination on the ground of religion is prohibited, so no community can be treated as inferior.

The state may intervene in religious matters to ensure equality — for example, by abolishing untouchability and making laws for social reform. India is therefore not anti-religious: the state keeps a principled distance from religion.

qa.q: Explain the relationship between caste and politics in India.
a: **Caste in politics:** parties take caste into account while choosing candidates, since the dominant caste of a constituency influences the result; voters' preferences are shaped by caste; and governments are formed keeping caste arithmetic in mind.

**Politics in caste:** politics has sharpened caste identities — castes have formed associations and asserted themselves to claim a share of political power, which is how OBCs and Dalits entered politics in large numbers.

**But caste is not everything:** no parliamentary constituency has a majority of one caste, so every party must appeal across castes; no caste votes as a single block; and voters also judge the government's performance and the leader. Caste inequality persists, but caste alone does not win an election.

qa.q: Name any three steps taken to increase women's representation in India.
qa.a: One-third of the seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women, and several states have raised this to half, so more than a million women now hold elected positions in local bodies. In 2023 Parliament passed the 106th Constitutional Amendment reserving one-third of the seats in the Lok Sabha and the state assemblies for women, to take effect after the next census and delimitation. The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 — equal wages for equal work — supports women's participation outside the home as well.

title: Political Parties
short: Functions of parties, national parties, and reforms.
lede: One list of functions, one list of national parties with symbols, and one list of challenges with matching reforms.
lens: **3–5 marks.** The functions of political parties and the challenges they face are asked almost every year.
Recognised national parties and their symbols are a quick, certain 3 marks if learned exactly.
concepts: **1. What is a political party?** A group of people who come together to **contest elections and hold power** in the government. A party agrees on some policies and programmes for the society with a view to promoting the collective good, decides what policies to pursue once in power, and reflects fundamental political divisions in a society by standing for a particular ideology. A party has three parts: the **leaders**, the **active members** and the **followers**.

**2. Why parties are necessary.** In a large society representative government needs an agency that gathers a wide range of views and presents them to the government; parties perform this function. Without them, every candidate would be independent, no one could promise any major policy change, and no one would be responsible for how the country is run.

**3. Functions of political parties.** (a) **Contest elections** — candidates are selected either by the members and supporters or by the top leaders; in India, top party leaders usually select the candidates. (b) **Put forward different policies and programmes** — voters get to choose between them. (c) **Play a decisive role in making laws** — since legislatures have many members, laws are debated and passed along party lines, so the party leadership effectively decides. (d) **Form and run the government** — the party or coalition that wins forms the government, and the top party leaders become ministers. (e) **Play the role of opposition** — parties that lose elections voice different views and criticise the government for its failures or wrong policies; they also mobilise opposition to the government. (f) **Shape public opinion** — parties raise and highlight issues through their members, workers and pressure groups. (g) **Provide access to government machinery and welfare schemes** — ordinary citizens approach local party leaders for help.

**4. National parties of India.** A party is recognised as a **national party** if it secures at least **6% of the total votes in Lok Sabha or Assembly elections in four states** and wins at least **four seats in the Lok Sabha**. The recognised national parties, with their symbols:

**5. State parties.** A party that is recognised as a state party if it secures at least **6% of the total votes in the Legislative Assembly of a state and wins at least two seats**. Examples include the Samajwadi Party, Rashtriya Janata Dal, Biju Janata Dal, YSR Congress, Shiromani Akali Dal, DMK and AIADMK.

**6. Challenges to political parties.** (a) **Lack of internal democracy** — power is concentrated in a few top leaders, there are no organisational elections, no membership registers, and ordinary members do not get enough information. (b) **Dynastic succession** — top positions are controlled by members of one family, which is unfair to other members and undemocratic. (c) **Money and muscle power** — parties grow more concerned with winning elections than with principles, so they nominate candidates who can raise money, and sometimes criminals with cases against them. (d) **Lack of meaningful choice** — parties do not offer significantly different policies or ideologies, and many leaders shift between parties, so voters have little real alternative.

**7. Reforms.** The **Constitution was amended to prevent defection** — an elected representative cannot change parties to become a minister or for cash reward; every candidate must file an **affidavit** giving details of property and pending criminal cases; parties must hold **organisational elections** and file **income tax returns**; the **Election Commission** has ordered parties to give tickets on the basis of merit, to keep accounts and to submit audited statements; and the **anti-defection law** and the **Right to Information** have increased transparency. Suggestions also include a law to regulate internal party affairs and reservation for women in party posts.
tricks: - **National party test: 6% of votes in four states + 4 Lok Sabha seats. State party: 6% + 2 Assembly seats.** *'Four for national, two for state.'*
- **Seven functions in order:** contest, policies, laws, government, opposition, opinion, welfare.
- **Four challenges:** internal democracy, dynasty, money and muscle, no real choice — each pairs with a reform.
mistakes: - Giving the BSP symbol as the elephant with a howdah or naming a party that is only a state party. Stick to the EC's recognised national party list.
- Saying the anti-defection law stops all defection. It bars changing parties **to become a minister or for cash reward**; splits and mergers are treated differently.
- Forgetting that candidates must file an **affidavit** — that is a marked point in the reforms answer.

qa.q: What is the criterion for a party to be recognised as a national party?
qa.a: A party is recognised as a national party by the Election Commission if it secures at least six per cent of the total votes in Lok Sabha elections or Assembly elections in four states, and wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha. State parties need at least six per cent of the votes in the state Assembly elections and at least two seats.

qa.q: Describe the main functions of political parties in a democracy.
a: **Contesting elections:** parties select candidates and campaign for them; in India, top leaders usually choose the candidates.
**Putting forward policies and programmes:** parties present different sets of policies, and voters choose between them.
**Making laws:** legislatures have many members, so laws are debated and passed along party lines, and the party leadership effectively decides.
**Forming and running the government:** the winning party or coalition forms the government, and its top leaders become ministers and run the administration.
**Playing the opposition:** losing parties criticise the government for its failures and wrong policies, mobilise opposition and voice different views.
**Shaping public opinion:** parties raise and highlight issues through lakhs of members and workers and through pressure groups.
**Providing access to government machinery and welfare schemes:** people approach local party leaders to get work done or to access government programmes.

qa.q: What are the main challenges faced by political parties in India? Suggest any three reforms.
a: **Challenges:** (1) **Lack of internal democracy** — power is concentrated in the hands of a few top leaders, there are no regular organisational elections or membership registers, and ordinary members lack information; (2) **Dynastic succession** — top posts are controlled by family members of the leaders, which is unfair and undemocratic; (3) **Money and muscle power** — parties nominate candidates who can raise money and sometimes candidates with criminal cases, because winning matters more than principles; (4) **Lack of meaningful choice** — parties offer very similar policies and ideologies, and leaders shift freely between parties.

**Reforms:** the constitution was amended to prevent **defection**, so elected representatives cannot change parties for ministerial posts or cash; every candidate must file an **affidavit** declaring property and pending criminal cases, which the Supreme Court made mandatory; parties must hold **organisational elections** and file **income tax returns**; and the Election Commission has ordered parties to keep audited accounts and to distribute tickets on merit.

qa.q: How do political parties shape public opinion?
qa.a: Parties raise and highlight issues through their lakhs of members and workers spread over the country, and through the pressure groups they support. They also use newspapers, meetings and social media to explain their stand. When a party is not able to solve a problem, it highlights the issue and mobilises opposition, which forces the government to respond.

title: Outcomes of Democracy
short: Accountability, economic growth, dignity and the case against dictatorship.
lede: The most conceptual chapter in Polity. Every answer is a claim plus a reason — practise writing claim-reason pairs.
lens: **3–5 marks.** 'Democracy is better than dictatorship because…' and the outcomes on economic growth and dignity are the set questions.
This chapter is also where **case-based/source-based** questions are most likely — a passage or a statement followed by three questions.
concepts: **1. How to assess democracy.** People's expectations from democracy are enormous, which makes the assessment difficult. The standard test: a democratic government must be **accountable, responsive and legitimate**. **Accountability** means citizens have the right to examine how decisions are made, so democracy must follow norms and procedures and give people a right to information. **Responsiveness** means the government must attend to the needs and expectations of citizens. **Legitimacy** means the government is the people's own government, elected by them — which is why even where democracy performs poorly it is still preferred, because it cannot be dismissed as illegitimate.

**2. Democracy versus dictatorship on efficiency.** A democratic government may be slower, less efficient and not always very attentive to the will of the people, because decisions involve **consultation and negotiation** among many. But this deliberation **reduces the chance of rash or irresponsible decisions**, and it makes decisions more acceptable to the people. A dictatorship may take quicker decisions because it does not have to consult anyone, but those decisions are not necessarily better and are often not acceptable.

**3. Economic growth and development.** Studies of the rate of economic growth between 1950 and 2000 show that **dictatorships had a slightly higher rate of growth** than democracies overall, but the difference is small. Among the poorer countries, democracies have caught up with dictatorships in recent decades. **Economic growth depends on many factors** — the country's population size, the global situation, cooperation from other countries and the economic priorities adopted by the ruling party — so democracy cannot be blamed for slower growth. Inequality is a real problem in democracies: a small number of ultra-rich enjoy a disproportionate share of wealth, and those at the bottom find it very difficult to meet basic needs. **But** democracies at least make it possible to raise the issue, and governments can and do act on it, whereas a dictatorship hides the gap.

**4. Reduction of inequality and poverty.** Democracy has not been able to eliminate poverty, and in some countries poverty has grown. Even so, democratic governments in India have introduced a range of schemes for the poor, and the fact that poverty can be openly discussed and campaigned about is itself a democratic outcome. In non-democratic states, inequality may be lower on paper but the reasons are not debated and the poor have no voice.

**5. Accommodation of social diversity.** Democracy is the best form of government to accommodate social diversity because it develops **procedures to conduct competition** among different groups, so that competition does not become explosive. It **gives due representation** to different castes, religions and linguistic groups, and it recognises that the interests of the majority are not always the same as those of a particular community. Democracy requires the majority to work with the minority so that any group can form a majority; it therefore respects differences and provides a **mechanism to negotiate differences**. Democracies worldwide have shown that they can develop procedures to accommodate diversity — although there is much more to be done in India, where demands of caste and religious groups still lead to conflict.

**6. Dignity and freedom of citizens.** This is the most fundamental outcome. Democracy is based on the recognition of the equal worth of all citizens, so it treats everyone with dignity and respect. Women, who were treated as subordinate, have gained the legal right to equality and have won their way into public life. The claims of disadvantaged and discriminated castes for equal status and equal opportunity are strengthened by democracy. **Democracy stands much superior in promoting the dignity and freedom of the citizen** — and the passion for respect and freedom is the basis of democracy, which is why people will not accept being ruled by unelected leaders.

**7. Democracy's own examination.** Democracy allows people to examine its functioning and criticise it, and this criticism is itself a sign of its strength. The fact that people keep complaining that democracy is not working shows that people have become more aware and expect more from democracy — which is exactly what a healthy democracy needs.
tricks: - **Three words for assessment: accountable, responsive, legitimate.** Any 5-mark answer can be organised around them.
- **Growth question = 'dictatorships grew slightly faster, but the difference is small and growth depends on other factors'.** Give both halves.
- **Dignity is the *most fundamental* outcome.** If a question asks which outcome is basic, that is the answer.
mistakes: - Saying democracies always grow faster. The evidence is that dictatorships had a **slightly higher** average rate; the difference is small.
- Writing that democracy has eliminated inequality. It has not — the honest answer is that it makes inequality **visible and actionable**.
- Treating criticism of democracy as a weakness. It is a **strength**: only democracy can be publicly criticised.

qa.q: Why is a democratic government regarded as legitimate?
qa.a: Because it is the people's own government, chosen by them through regular, free and fair elections. Even where democracy performs poorly or is slow, it cannot be dismissed as illegitimate, because the authority to govern comes from the consent of the governed. A dictatorship may be more efficient, but it is never the people's own government.

qa.q: 'Democracy is a better form of government than dictatorship.' Support the statement with five arguments.
a: **It is accountable and responsive** — citizens can examine how decisions are made, and the government must attend to their needs.
**It improves the quality of decision-making** — consultation and negotiation among many people reduce the chance of rash or irresponsible decisions.
**It provides a method to deal with differences and conflicts** — competition is conducted through agreed procedures rather than through force, so social diversity can be accommodated.
**It enhances the dignity of citizens** — it recognises the equal worth of all, and gives women and disadvantaged castes legal equality and a voice.
**It allows its own mistakes to be corrected** — a democratic government can be replaced at the next election, and public criticism of its functioning is allowed; a dictatorship hides its errors.

qa.q: How does democracy produce an accountable, responsive and legitimate government?
a: **Accountable:** citizens have the right to examine the process of decision-making and to hold the government to account; democracy follows norms and procedures, and citizens have legal rights such as the right to information.
**Responsive:** the government must attend to the needs and expectations of the people, and if it fails to do so it can be voted out; regular elections force governments to respond.

**Legitimate:** the government is elected by the people and is therefore the people's own government, so even a slow or inefficient democratic government is preferred to a dictatorship that is not answerable to anyone.

**Supporting evidence:** despite many problems, democracies around the world have survived and people have continued to prefer them, which shows that legitimacy is what ultimately sustains a government.

qa.q: Why does democracy stand superior to other forms of government in promoting the dignity and freedom of citizens?
qa.a: Because democracy is based on the recognition of the equal worth of all citizens. It gives legal equality to women and to disadvantaged and discriminated castes, and it allows people to claim respect and freedom openly. In a non-democratic state, the claims of women and of disadvantaged groups cannot be raised publicly, so their dignity is not legally protected.

qa.q: Why is it wrong to blame democracy for slower economic growth?
qa.a: Because the rate of economic growth depends on many factors other than the form of government — the country's population size, the global economic situation, cooperation from other countries and the economic priorities chosen by the ruling party. Studies show that the difference in growth rates between democracies and dictatorships is small, and among poorer countries democracies have caught up with dictatorships in recent decades.

Why the mistake costs marks: Saying democracies always grow faster. The evidence is that dictatorships had a slightly higher average rate; the difference is small.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A Class 10 student is preparing “Outcomes of Democracy”. Their note says: How to assess democracy. People's expectations from democracy are enormous, which makes the assessment difficult. The standard test: a democratic government must be accountable, responsive and legitimate. Accountability means citizens have the right to examine how decisions are made, so democracy mu

The chapter is described as: Accountability, economic growth, dignity and the case against dictatorship..

(a) Name the key idea.
(b) How is this usually asked in the paper?
(c) State one mistake that would cost a mark.
a: (a) Accountability, economic growth, dignity and the case against dictatorship.
(b) –5 marks. 'Democracy is better than dictatorship because…' and the outcomes on economic growth and dignity are the set questions.
(c) Saying democracies always grow faster. The evidence is that dictatorships had a slightly higher average rate; the difference is small.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Two students attempt: “Why is a democratic government regarded as legitimate?” Student A writes one line. Student B writes points, an example and a check.

(a) Which answer frame should you use for full marks?
(b) Write the model points.
(c) Add one memory trick you would use on exam morning.
a: (a) Statement → working or reasons in points → example or check. One-line answers lose step marks.

(b) Because it is the people's own government, chosen by them through regular, free and fair elections. Even where democracy performs poorly or is slow, it cannot be dismissed as illegitimate, because the authority to govern comes from the consent of the governed. A dictatorship may be more efficient, but it is never the people's own government.
(c) Three words for assessment: accountable, responsive, legitimate. Any 5-mark answer can be organised around them.

mcq.q: Which of the following is the most fundamental outcome of democracy? (a) faster economic growth (b) promotion of the dignity and freedom of the citizen (c) efficient decision-making (d) absence of conflict
mcq.a: **(b) promotion of the dignity and freedom of the citizen** — democracy is based on recognising the equal worth of all citizens.

mcq.q: Democracy is better than dictatorship mainly because it: (a) takes decisions faster (b) is more efficient (c) is accountable, responsive and legitimate (d) has no opposition
mcq.a: **(c)** — accountability, responsiveness and legitimacy are the standard tests of a democratic government.

mcq.q: Criticism of the functioning of democracy by citizens is: (a) a sign of its weakness (b) a sign of its strength and of people's rising expectations (c) proof that democracy fails (d) irrelevant
mcq.a: **(b)** — only democracy can be publicly criticised, and complaint shows that people expect more of it.

mcq.q: The most exam-ready way to revise “Outcomes of Democracy” is: (a) read the heading only  (b) learn the key idea plus one example  (c) skip written practice  (d) memorise a random extra topic
mcq.a: **(b) learn the key idea plus one example.** The chapter is Accountability, economic growth, dignity and the case against dictatorship..

mcq.q: A 3-mark answer on “Outcomes of Democracy” should: (a) be one sentence  (b) start with the idea, then a reason or method  (c) copy the whole chapter  (d) leave the example out
mcq.a: **(b) start with the idea, then a reason or method.** Step marks follow that frame.

trend: One 5-mark question on the outcomes of democracy is virtually certain, and this chapter is the usual source of case-based or source-based questions with three short parts.
onepager: - Test: accountable, responsive, legitimate.
- Growth: dictatorships slightly faster, difference small; growth depends on population, global situation and policy.
- Democracy accommodates diversity by turning competition into agreed procedures.
- Dignity and freedom of the citizen is the most fundamental outcome.
- Public criticism of democracy is evidence of its strength.
task: Write five claim-reason pairs on index cards — for example 'democracy is legitimate / because it is elected by the people'. Shuffle them and match them under time pressure; the exam question is exactly this matching exercise with two marks per pair.
